title: Restoring Hope in a Hopeless Generation
excerpt: A full Sunday Service message from Romans 4:13–20 on restoring hope in a generation facing impossible circumstances: God speaks in the impossible, hope is built on His promises, and hope in God refuses to give up.
content:
“Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed…” — Romans 4:18

What does it mean to have hope when everything around you seems to give you a reason to give up? In this Sunday Service message, the church was called back to a hope that is not controlled by circumstances—a hope anchored in God and in what He has spoken.

“Hope is the confidence that tomorrow can be better than today.”

The central biblical example was Abraham in Romans 4:13–20. God had made him a promise, yet the circumstances surrounding that promise eventually looked naturally impossible. Abraham’s story therefore became a picture of what it means to live by hope and faith in a generation that can easily become discouraged.

Abraham: Against All Hope, He Believed

Romans 4 presents Abraham as a man who had received a promise from God. The fulfilment was not based merely on what Abraham could accomplish for himself. His confidence rested in the God who had spoken.

Then Scripture gives the striking description:

“Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed…” — Romans 4:18

There was a contradiction between what Abraham could see naturally and what God had promised. Yet he continued believing. The sermon used that tension to speak to students and young people whose circumstances may appear to contradict their prayers, expectations, calling or future.

Hope is therefore not merely excitement when things are going well. Hope becomes especially important when the visible situation appears hopeless.

1. God Speaks in the Impossible

The first major lesson from Abraham was that God speaks in the impossible.

Abraham’s journey shows God calling and promising before Abraham could see how everything would be fulfilled. The story in Genesis 12 and Genesis 15 is therefore not simply about Abraham’s ability; it is about the faithfulness of the God who called him.

An impossible situation does not silence God. What looks finished to human eyes may still be a place where God speaks, calls, directs and gives a promise.

The congregation was challenged not to determine its entire future from its present circumstances. A difficult semester, a delayed answer, an uncertain career, a broken situation or what other people have said cannot automatically become the final word over a believer’s life.

The question becomes: What has God said?

2. Hope Is Built on God’s Promises

The second emphasis was that hope must have a foundation. Abraham’s hope was not built on favourable circumstances. It was built on the promise of God.

This distinction matters because circumstances change. Feelings change. People can change what they say about you. Situations that appear favourable today can become difficult tomorrow. But the sermon repeatedly brought the congregation back to trusting God.

The life of faith was presented as a journey requiring perseverance. There are moments when progress appears slow and moments when a person may be tempted to abandon what God has begun. The response of faith is to continue.

This was also applied practically to areas such as restoration of broken relationships. Hope does not immediately discard everything because something has become difficult. Where restoration is possible and consistent with God’s direction, hope allows a person to believe that what appears broken does not necessarily have to remain broken.

The message also echoed the posture of Philippians 3:12–14: not remaining trapped by what is behind, but continuing toward what lies ahead.

3. Hope in God Refuses to Give Up

The third major point returned directly to Romans 4:19–20.

Abraham did not deny the reality of his circumstances. Scripture says that he “faced the fact” that his body was as good as dead, since he was about one hundred years old, and that Sarah’s womb was also unable naturally to bear a child.

Yet Scripture immediately adds:

“Without weakening in his faith…” — Romans 4:19

And then:

“Yet he did not waver through unbelief regarding the promise of God…” — Romans 4:20

This establishes an important distinction: hope does not require denying the facts. Hope means refusing to allow the facts to displace faith in God’s promise.

Abraham could see the reality. He knew his age. He knew Sarah’s condition. Faith did not require pretending those things were absent. But the visible facts did not become greater than the God who had spoken.

The practical exhortation was therefore simple and forceful:

“Refuse to give up.”

Even when circumstances are unfavourable, even when other alternatives present themselves, the believer is called to remain in Christ and continue toward what God has ordained.

Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus

The message then moved into the historic hymn Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus. Its place in the service reinforced the call to perseverance, courage and remaining steadfast in Christ rather than surrendering when opposition comes.

View the hymn reference and history →

The congregation was reminded of Isaiah 54:17—“No weapon formed against you shall prosper.” The prayer was directed against anything seeking to hinder progress toward what God has called and ordained His people to become.

“You must become what God said you shall become.”

Do Not Entertain Unbelief

The preacher then returned again to Romans 4:20:

“Yet he did not waver through unbelief regarding the promises of God.”

The emphasis was that Abraham did not entertain unbelief concerning what God had promised. Once God had spoken, Abraham’s response was to continue trusting Him.

“As far as God has said it, O God… I will trust You. I will believe You.”

That became a personal question for everyone listening:

What has God said concerning your life?

In regard to what God has said, the response of faith is not to entertain unbelief. The preacher illustrated this with the language of Psalm 23: even when walking through the valley and the shadow of death, fear does not have to determine how a believer sees God.

“Challenges will not make me change my mind concerning how I see God. The challenges, the situation will not change my love for God.”

A Prayer for a Younger Generation

The sermon then moved from teaching into intercession. The preacher expressed a particular prayer for the younger generation: that God would restore their hope and restore what had been lost.

“My brothers, my sisters, our expectation shall not be cut off.”

This echoed the promise of Proverbs 23:18—there is a future, and hope or expectation will not be cut off.

The declaration was repeated over the congregation:

“I declare in the name of Jesus Christ that your hope and your expectation shall not be cut off.”

The congregation was asked to stand. The prayer became intensely personal. Each person was called to pray for his or her own life—not merely to participate because everyone else was praying.

“Let them cut everything else and not our hope in God. Let them remove everything else, and our hope in God will not be cut off.”

Abraham trusted God, and the congregation was being called to that same posture: a hope in Christ that remains unshaken by circumstances.

You Are What God Says About You

Another major declaration emerged during the prayer:

“You are not what people say about you. You are what God says about you.”

The preacher prayed that young people would not surrender their hope because of circumstances or because of words spoken about them by other people.

The prayer increasingly focused on destiny. The congregation called upon God concerning their future and asked that discouragement would not separate them from what God had purposed for them.

The central prayer could be summarized in the words repeated throughout the altar moment:

“May my hope in God not be cut off. May my hope remain unshaken.”

From Personal Hope to Seeking the Lost

The closing movement of the service did not leave hope as something private. The preacher turned the restored congregation outward toward students who were absent, discouraged, spiritually distant or lost.

“We must go ahead. We must leave the 99 and go for one.”

This reflects Jesus’ picture of the shepherd seeking the one who is lost in Luke 15:3–7 and Matthew 18:12–14.

The challenge was practical. Do not merely speak generally about lost students. Think of someone. Call that person. Reach that brother. Reach that sister. Reach that student.

“Call that brother. Call that sister from wherever she is.”

The church was being commissioned to carry hope beyond the people already gathered in the service. A generation whose hope has been restored must become a generation willing to carry hope to somebody else.

Prayer Against Hopelessness

The service then entered its final corporate prayer. The congregation prayed directly against hopelessness, pessimism, discouragement and the spirit of giving up.

The prayer moved through the areas in which students often feel pressure: life, studies, career, destiny and the future.

“Any hopelessness… any pessimism, spirit of giving up…”

Rather than agreeing with hopelessness, the congregation was instructed to declare victory and confidence in God.

“I declare my victory.”
“I shall make it in my career.”
“My destiny is secure.”
“My future is secure.”

The final corporate declaration placed the congregation’s destiny and future in God’s hands, concluding in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The service then closed with the congregation shouting and appreciating God.

The Message to Carry Home

Restoring Hope in a Hopeless Generation ultimately returned again and again to Abraham. He faced facts that appeared impossible, but he did not allow those facts to remove his confidence in the God who had spoken.

For the student facing uncertainty, for the believer waiting for restoration, for the person tempted to give up, and for the generation surrounded by discouragement, the sermon’s call remains:

God speaks in the impossible.

Hope is built on God’s promises.

Hope in God refuses to give up.

And once that hope has been restored, it must move outward: leave the ninety-nine and go for the one.

Key Scriptures from the Message

  • Romans 4:13–20 — Abraham believes God’s promise against all hope.
  • Genesis 12; 15 — God calls Abraham and establishes His promise.
  • Philippians 3:12–14 — Pressing forward toward the goal.
  • Psalm 23 — Trusting God even through the valley.
  • Isaiah 54:17 — No weapon formed against God’s people shall prosper.
  • Proverbs 23:18 — There is a future, and hope will not be cut off.
  • Luke 15:3–7; Matthew 18:12–14 — Leaving the ninety-nine to seek the one.
